title: Water conservation and environmental release for aquariums
audience: Aquarium maintenance workers who carry out partial water changes, top-ups and tank drain-downs, and who handle tank water, sand, rock and plants during a service
learningOutcomes: Separate evaporation from a leak in a tank by running a bucket test and recording the result
Carry out routine partial water changes on the owner's plan schedule, and make extra changes only where the test results or the plan call for them
Refuse to release tank water, sand, rock, plants or animals to stormwater, a waterway or bushland without an approved route and any permit the state requires
Record the volume moved, the route, the approval and the person who approved it
referencesAtStart: Official sources for this lesson: NSW Department of Primary Industries, Aquarium owners and trade (no date shown); Queensland Government, Your legal obligation for invasive freshwater animals (last updated 28 May 2026); NSW Legislation, Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act 1979 No 200, section 11 (no in-force date shown in the extract; amendments listed up to 2024 No 85).

instruction.heading: Why tank water loss and water changes cost money
instruction.body: Every litre lost from a tank has to be replaced, and each top-up or water change changes the temperature, the salinity and the chemistry that the animals live in. Evaporation from an open tank on a warm, dry day is normal. A steady loss on a cool, still night can point to a leak, a worn seal, a misaligned overflow or a splash from the filter outlet. Water changes that the plan does not call for cost money, add stress for the animals, and can disturb the bacteria that keep the tank stable. Cost reduction starts with finding the cause of the loss, rather than topping up at every visit without knowing why.

instruction.heading: The bucket test
instruction.body: A bucket test separates evaporation from a leak. Fill a bucket with tank water, stand it in the tank so that its water level is close to the tank level, and mark the level inside and outside the bucket at the start. Leave it for the same period and compare the two marks. If the tank has dropped more than the water in the bucket, the loss is more likely a leak or an overflow problem, and it should be reported. The method is a practical technique and not a certified test. Record the weather, the times and the result.

instruction.heading: Routine water changes, extra changes and new water
instruction.body: Routine partial water changes are a normal part of aquarium care, and they follow the schedule in the owner's plan. Extra changes are made only where the test results, the plan or a qualified specialist calls for one, and the reason is recorded each time. Match the temperature and, for a marine tank, the salinity of the new water to the tank before it goes in. Tap water must have chlorine and chloramine removed before it is added to a tank, because both harm fish and the bacteria in the filter. Use a conditioner at the dose on its label, and check the label for the dechlorination method. Add new water slowly and away from the animals. Do not add water from an unknown source, such as a dam, a bore, a natural waterway or the sea, without first checking the state rules with the regulator.

instruction.heading: Releasing tank water, sand, rock, plants and animals
instruction.body: Tank water, sand, rock, plants and animals should not be released into stormwater, a kerb drain, a gutter, bushland or a waterway until a route is confirmed. Confirming the route with the client, the council and the water authority is practice in this draft, not a rule read from an official page. For animals, the rules are stricter. In New South Wales, the Department of Primary Industries says that listed prohibited and notifiable species may not be kept, purchased, sold or transported, and that releasing fish into public waters needs a fish stocking permit (no date shown). In Queensland, listed prohibited species must not be held or brought in, and a person who has or suspects one should inform Biosecurity Queensland without delay (last updated 28 May 2026). Do not release, donate or sell an animal under this lesson, and do not move plants or live rock between tanks or sites without checking the rules. Do not assume that any discharge route is allowed.

instruction.heading: Recording tank water movements
instruction.body: Record the volume drained, changed or topped up where you know it, the route, the approval or permit relied on, the time, the reason and the person who approved the move. Where the route is unknown, stop and refer rather than moving the water. A record that shows an approved route protects the business and the client. A record that shows the water went somewhere unknown protects neither.

procedure: Check the reason for any water loss, and run a bucket test where the cause is not clear.
Record the weather, the start and finish times, and the water levels.
Report any suspected leak or overflow fault to the client, and refer the repair.
Make the routine partial water change on the owner's plan schedule, and any extra change that the test results call for. Record the reason for each change.
Treat new water as the label and the owner's plan direct, and match its temperature and, for marine tanks, its salinity.
Confirm the release route with the client, the council and the water authority before moving any water, sand, rock or plants.
Do not release, sell or donate any animal. Refer any animal removal to the client and to the state rules for the species.
Record the volume, the route, the approval or permit and the person who approved it. Wear the PPE set by {{business:safety.required_ppe}} when handling sludge and sand.

workedExamples.situation: A client asks you to drain a marine tank into the stormwater drain outside because the water looks cloudy and they want the tank cleaned quickly.
workedExamples.reasoning: Do not drain into the stormwater drain. Record the request, the refusal and the referral. If the cloudiness calls for a water change, the owner's plan decides the volume and the treated water used, and the change is recorded.

workedExamples.situation: A client in New South Wales asks you to take a surplus goldfish from their tank and release it into a nearby creek, because the fish is healthy and they do not want to keep it.
workedExamples.reasoning: Refuse the release. The NSW Department of Primary Industries says that releasing fish into public waters needs a fish stocking permit (no date shown), and that page links discarding an unwanted fish to section 11 of the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act 1979 (no in-force date shown in the extract; amendments listed to 2024 No 85). Record the request and the refusal, and refer the client to the state rules for rehoming the fish. Do not take the fish away to release it yourself.

equipmentAndPpe: Bucket for the bucket test, and a marker for the water level
Water conditioner and product label for the dechlorination method
Sealed container for holding sand, rock or sludge on site
Gloves, eye protection and footwear with grip, as set by {{business:safety.required_ppe}}

commonErrors.error: Topping up or changing water at every visit without finding the cause of a repeat loss.
commonErrors.prevention: Run a bucket test, record the weather and the result, and report a suspected leak.

commonErrors.error: Draining tank water to stormwater or a drain without a confirmed route.
commonErrors.prevention: Confirm the route with the client, the council and the water authority in writing before moving any water.

commonErrors.error: Releasing an animal, or moving live rock or plants to another site, because the client asks.
commonErrors.prevention: Refuse the release or movement, check the state rules, and record the request and the refusal.

commonErrors.error: Adding new water that is at a different temperature or salinity from the tank.
commonErrors.prevention: Match temperature and, for marine tanks, salinity before the new water goes in.

commonErrors.error: Skipping the routine partial water change in the plan because the tank looks clear.
commonErrors.prevention: Follow the plan's schedule, and record any change to it with the reason.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: The New South Wales Department of Primary Industries says that listed prohibited and notifiable species may not be kept, purchased, sold or transported, and that releasing fish into public waters needs a fish stocking permit (no date shown). This lesson does not grant any permit, and completing it does not authorise any release.
Queensland: listed prohibited species must not be held or brought in, and a person who has or suspects one should inform Biosecurity Queensland without delay (last updated 28 May 2026).
Confirming the route with the council and the water authority before any discharge is practice in this draft.

qualityStandard: A bucket test or other cause check is recorded before a top-up is made on a repeat loss
Every routine or extra water change is recorded with its reason, and matches the owner's plan
No water, sand, rock, plant or animal leaves the site without a confirmed route and any approval or permit recorded
New water is matched to the tank's temperature and, for marine tanks, salinity before it is added
documentationEvidence: Bucket test record with weather, times, levels and result
Water change or top-up record with volume, temperature match and the reason
Release route, approval or permit reference, and the approving person
Referral note for any suspected leak, overflow fault or refused release
summary: Find the cause of water loss with a bucket test before topping up at a repeat loss.
Change water on the owner's plan schedule, and make extra changes only where the results or the plan call for them. Match the new water to the tank.
Do not release tank water, sand, rock, plants or animals without a confirmed route and any permit the state requires.
Record the volume, the route, the approval and the approving person for every movement.

knowledgeChecks.question: A client wants a marine tank drained into the stormwater drain outside. What should you do first?
options: Drain it, because it is only salty water and it will not harm the stormwater system at all
Drain it at night when nobody is watching, so the neighbours do not notice the discharge
Drain it after adding a dechlorinator, so the water is safe for the stormwater system to take
Confirm the approved route with the client, the council and the water authority, and record the request

knowledgeChecks.question: A client asks you to release a surplus aquarium fish into a local NSW creek. What is the correct response?
options: Release it, because the fish is healthy and the creek has plenty of room for one more animal today
Refuse. Release into NSW public waters needs a fish stocking permit, and dumping an unwanted fish is an offence
Release it if the fish is small enough, since small fish are not covered by the stocking rules
Release it, because the client has signed a form that takes full responsibility for the release on the day

knowledgeChecks.question: Why should unneeded partial water changes be avoided?
options: Each unneeded change adds cost and stress and can disturb the tank, so extra changes should be made only where the results or the plan show a need
Water changes never help a tank in any situation at all, so they should be avoided as a general rule for every visit and every client
Water changes break the filter, so the bacteria die off and the tank must be started again from scratch after every single change made by the crew
Water changes are banned in every state and territory in Australia, so any change made by a contractor is always an offence under the law

officialReferences.title: Aquarium owners and trade
officialReferences.covers: NSW Department of Primary Industries, Aquarium owners and trade (no date shown). The page says to check which species are illegal to possess, buy, sell or move; that releasing fish into NSW public waters is illegal without a fish stocking permit under the Fisheries Management Act; that buying fish, plants or live rock from overseas on the internet is illegal; and that dumping an unwanted pet fish is an illegal act. It names the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act 1979 for animal welfare. The page uses the word illegal for these points, not warning. Publisher: NSW Department of Primary Industries.

officialReferences.title: Your legal obligation for invasive freshwater animals
officialReferences.covers: Open the page; it refers to the Biosecurity Regulation 2016 for the full list of prohibited species and says whom to contact about a suspected one. It does not name aquarium species or set a release rule for aquarium fish. Publisher: Queensland Government.
